title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior research demonstrates that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings while separate work on verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers shows that post‑generation checks reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

High‑level contribution and key finding. We provide (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reusing a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run. We derive concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations grounded in the archived traces.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Prior intent‑to‑configuration work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds (intent‑based translation, PreConfig, GraphSynth) but typically evaluates generation quality rather than end‑to‑end staged rollout safety. Verifier‑guided loops and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning approaches (e.g., TerraFormer) report correctness gains in IaC and provisioning contexts; these motivate analogous integrations for NetOps but do not demonstrate production‑scale closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts. Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space style, Kubernetes reachability analyses) are effective at finding configuration errors in emulated and offline settings, though tool scope and modeling assumptions differ. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) expand functionality for AIOps/RCA tasks but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and reviews repeatedly note an evaluation gap: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility under those constraints and to surface practical design pitfalls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and shared generation. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This choice intentionally isolates the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions. Because one generator call served both episodes for each pair, model_calls_used = 400 while planned episodes = 800; we describe this mapping to avoid reader confusion about model‑call accounting.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, difficulty metadata, and deterministic replay. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; any pair failing replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded per the missingness_plan. In this run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400).

Confirmatory and secondary analysis procedures. The primary analysis used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05). The exact McNemar test was reported for corroboration. Secondary outcomes included bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts; preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating excluded pairs as failures or restricted permutations) were available but unnecessary because there were no exclusions. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived in the analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts were baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts.

Repair and rollback observations. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Task difficulty metadata and representative patterns. Each task record includes a difficulty level label. Representative sample entries in the archived task manifest illustrate benchmark diversity (example: among the first six representative tasks the manifest records one medium, two hard, and three very_hard patterns). The full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 tasks are archived in the execution task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and can be aggregated by auditors; we do not invent aggregated counts here but the per‑task labels are part of the public artifact bundle.

Statistical interpretation. The observed ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply to these results.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Consequences for power, inference, and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation relied on within‑pair variability that did not occur in this run. The observed ceiling thus invalidates the power rationale and collapses inferential uncertainty: exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the data but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design that preserved generator variance.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete implementation steps for future preregistered runs that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions:

1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair.

2) Distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; archived validator_trace entries show acceptance decisions and validation_before/after states—using a separate scorer preserves adjudication.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a controlled fraction of perturbation seeds guaranteed to produce nontrivial baseline failure rates to preserve power. The task manifest supports seeding and deterministic generation, enabling reproducible adversarial injection.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure the benchmark composition contains a sufficient proportion of tasks labeled very_hard to produce measurable baseline errors; difficulty metadata per task are archived and can be sampled deterministically.

5) Instrumented mitigation metrics: enable and record repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes (these fields are already present in validator_trace entries and repair logs in the artifact bundle).

These recommendations are implementable directly from the archived artifacts and validator traces and are sufficient to produce a future confirmatory design with preserved statistical signal.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, two practical lessons are immediate: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide the potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions by incorporating independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts produced by the run include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). These artifacts contain the seeds, deterministic replay checks, and the validator_trace records that underpin the diagnosis and recommendations above; auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

Final interpretive boundary. The null paired difference observed here is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design. It should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general. Instead, it illustrates how specific preregistered design choices (shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring) can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate generator×guard closed‑loop effects. Evaluations that wish to measure guard utility must preserve generator variance and independent adjudication as described above.

Disclosure Statement (mandatory): Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini (declared in the archived model configuration). Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints (selected pre‑lock by the Research Director) limited the work to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. Permitted tools and capabilities: hosted model API calls, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the master prompt autonomy constraints; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred (permitted by the track) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as final empirical evidence unless reproduced in the post‑lock run.

Limitations: (1) Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale. (2) Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. (3) Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility. (4) Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions. (5) Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited. (6) Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults were not exercised and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work. (7) Aggregated difficulty reporting: full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not invent aggregated counts absent explicit artifact summarization in the manuscript body.
